t: Caltrans Standard Specifications: structure and how to read them
s: What the Standard Specifications are, how they are organized, and how a project manager actually uses them on an electrical contract.
x: Caltrans Standard Specifications: structure and how to read them In one sentence: the Standard Specifications are the rulebook that applies to every Caltrans contract. They tell you how work must be done, what materials are acceptable, how it is measured and how you get paid. What they are Caltrans publishes the Standard Specifications as one large book that is updated every few years. Every contract you bid on names the edition that applies, and that edition is part of the contract — even though it is not printed in your bid package. The Standard Specifications are generic : they are written for every highway project in the state. What makes them specific to your job is the combination with: the special provisions , which modify and add to the specs for this project, the project plans , which show what to build and where, the standard plans es , which show standard details (pull boxes, foundations, conduit installation). When these documents disagree, a defined order of precedence decides which one wins. How the book is organized The specifications are divided into divisions , and each division into numbered sections . A reference such as 86 2.05 reads as Section 86, subsection 2, paragraph 05 . Part What it covers Why it matters to an electrical PM Sections 1–9 — General provisions Definitions, bidding, award, scope, control of work, legal relations, prosecution and progress, payment Submittals, schedule, change orders, payment and claims all live here Sections 10–16 — General construction Work zone and traffic control, water pollution control, environmental stewardship, existing facilities Every freeway job: lane closures, BMPs during trenching, protecting existing equipment Earthwork, concrete, paving sections Excavation and backfill, concrete, asphalt and concrete repair Trench backfill, foundations, pull box surrounds, patching after trenching Section 86 — Electrical systems (general) Requirements common to all electrical work: conduit, pull boxes, conductors, splicing, grounding, service, foundations, testing The section you will open most often Section 87 — Electrical systems (specific) Each system: signals, lighting, detection, ramp metering, traffic monitoring, communications, fiber optics Where system specific materials and tests are defined Section numbers follow the recent editions of the book. Always confirm against the edition named in your contract. Anatomy of a section Most sections follow the same pattern. Once you know it, you can find anything quickly: 1. General — scope, definitions, submittals required, quality control. 2. Materials — what is acceptable (standards, ratings, approved products). 3. Construction — how to install it. 4. Payment — how the item is measured and paid (per linear foot, each, lump sum). For a PM, the two parts you read first are Submittals (what you must send before ordering or installing) and Payment (what you are actually paid for, and what is included in another item at no extra cost). How a PM uses them day to day Bidding: read the payment clause for each bid item so you know what is included in the price — for example, whether trenching and backfill are paid separately or included in the conduit item. Preconstruction: list every submittal the relevant sections require and build the submittal log from it. See submittals. Procurement: check the Materials subsections before you request quotes, so the supplier quotes a product that will be approved. See procurement long lead. In the field: when the crew asks "how deep?" or "what backfill?", the answer is in the Construction subsection — unless the special provisions or plans say otherwise. Testing and closeout: the required tests and documentation are listed in the sections; they become your acceptance checklist. See acceptance testing punch list. t: Special Provisions: what they change and why they win
s: What the Special Provisions are, how they relate to the Standard Specifications, and how a project manager reads them on a Caltrans electrical job.
x: Special Provisions: what they change and why they win In one sentence: the Special Provisions are the part of the contract written for this project. They change, delete and add to the standard specifications, and when the two disagree, the Special Provisions govern. Where they fit Every Caltrans contract is built from the same rulebook, the Standard Specifications, plus documents written for the job. The Special Provisions are the most important of those project documents. They arrive in the bid package (in the Notice to Bidders and Special Provisions book), together with the project plans and the bid forms. Together, the Special Provisions, the Revised Standard Specifications and the Standard Specifications make up the contract specifications . You never read one without the others. What is inside Special Provisions are organized with the same section numbers as the Standard Specifications, so Section 86 of the Special Provisions talks about the same subject as Section 86 of the book. Inside, you will typically find: Replacements: a paragraph of the Standard Specifications is replaced with new wording. Additions: new paragraphs or new subsections, for work the book doesn't cover or covers differently. Deletions: a requirement of the book that doesn't apply to this job. Project specific information: working days, liquidated damages, the DBE goal, the edition of the Standard Specifications and Standard Plans that applies, and any Revised Standard Plans. Most of the text is not written from scratch. Caltrans maintains Standard Special Provisions (SSPs) , standard wording that designers pick and fill in. When no standard wording fits, the designer writes a non standard special provision (nSSP) . On electrical jobs, the nSSPs are where you usually find specific equipment: a particular cabinet, router, switch, camera or battery requirement. How a PM uses them At bid time: read Sections 86 and 87 of the Special Provisions before pricing anything. Approved products, testing requirements and payment rules often change there. For submittals: every "submit" in the Special Provisions adds a line to your submittal log, on top of what the Standard Specifications already require. See submittals. For procurement: an nSSP that names a specific product or performance requirement is a long lead warning. Ask suppliers early. See procurement long lead. In the field: when the crew's question is answered by the book, check that the Special Provisions don't say otherwise before giving the answer. Why they win The contract sets an order of precedence for when its parts disagree, and the Special Provisions sit at the top of it: they govern over the project plans, the Standard Specifications and the Standard Plans. That is why the rule "never read the Standard Specifications alone" matters so much. If the conflict is real and the order of precedence doesn't settle it, don't guess: send an RFI to the Resident Engineer and wait for a written answer. Section numbers and document names follow recent editions. Always confirm against the edition named in your contract.

t: Order of precedence: which contract document wins
s: When the Special Provisions, plans, Standard Specifications and Standard Plans disagree, Section 5-1.02 decides which one governs. Here is the order and how to use it.
x: Order of precedence: which contract document wins In one sentence: when two parts of a Caltrans contract disagree, Section 5 1.02 of the standard specifications lists which one governs, starting with the special provisions. The order Section 5 1.02 ( Contract Components , in Section 5, Control of Work ) lists the parts of the contract in the order they govern when there is a discrepancy: 1. Special Provisions 2. Project plans 3. Standard Specifications (as revised by the Revised Standard Specifications) 4. Revised Standard Plans 5. Standard Plans 6. Supplemental project information The same section adds one more rule: on a drawing, written numbers and notes govern over the graphics . If a dimension is written on the plan, use it; don't scale the drawing. What it means in practice Special Provisions over everything: if the Special Provisions call for a different pull box, conductor or test than the plans or the book, follow the Special Provisions. Project plans over the book and the Standard Plans: the plans show this job. If a detail on the project plans differs from the Standard Plan it refers to, the project plan wins. Revised Standard Plans over Standard Plans: when a Standard Plan sheet has been revised since the edition you are using, the revised sheet is included with the contract and replaces it. Supplemental project information last: reports and reference material (for example, geotechnical or utility information) inform the work but don't override the contract requirements above it. When the order isn't enough The order of precedence settles conflicts between documents. It doesn't settle: a requirement that is unclear rather than contradictory, a conflict inside one document, a conflict between the documents and what you find in the field (a utility where the conduit should go, a foundation that doesn't fit). In those cases, write an RFI to the Resident Engineer, describe the conflict with sheet and section references, and propose a solution. Keep working on what isn't affected, and don't build the disputed item until you have a written answer: work done on a guess may not be paid. A quick check before you build 1. Find the requirement in the Special Provisions (same section number as the book). 2. Check the project plans and their notes. 3. Check the Standard Specifications and any Revised Standard Specifications. 4. Check the Revised Standard Plans, then the Standard Plans. 5. Still unclear? RFI. Based on Section 5 1.02 of recent editions. Always confirm against the edition named in your contract.
